item.title: Rams hope to have Kobie Turner back for Week 12
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: Rams head coach Sean McVay shared a negative update on wide receiver Puka Nacua's health on Friday, but he had better news regarding defensive tackle Kobie Turner.
item.content:encoded:
Rams head coach Sean McVay shared a negative update on wide receiver Puka Nacua's health on Friday, but he had better news regarding defensive tackle Kobie Turner.

McVay said that the team is planning to activate defensive tackle Kobie Turner from injured reserve ahead of next Wednesday's game against the Packers. Turner has missed the last four games with a groin injury.

Turner had 22 tackles in six games before his injury.

Getting Turner back would give the Rams the full defensive front they envisioned when they traded for Myles Garrett and coaxed Aaron Donald out of retirement this offseason. With Nacua expected to miss the rest of the season and Davante Adams still out, they'll be banking on that defensive front being a major asset to their playoff push.

item.title: Todd Bowles: Baker Mayfield trending in the right direction to play vs. Lions
item.dc:creator: Myles Simmons
item.description: It sounds like the Buccaneers are planning to have quarterback Baker Mayfield start this weekend when they play the Lions.
item.content:encoded:
It sounds like the Buccaneers are planning to have quarterback Baker Mayfield start this weekend when they play the Lions.

Via Rick Stroud of the Tampa Bay Times, head coach Todd Bowles said on Friday that Mayfield is “trending in the right direction” to play on Sunday. The team will evaluate how Mayfield feels after practicing on Thursday and Friday.

While Bowles did not explicitly say it, Mayfield seems likely to be listed as questionable when game statuses are out later this afternoon.

Mayfield has dealt with a variety of injuries this season, but he is most impacted at the moment by a foot issue. He’s also currently listed on the injury report with a right thumb injury, though that is no longer preventing him from playing.

It’s been a lackluster 2026 for Mayfield after signing an extension with the Bucs just before the start of the regular season. He’s completed 60.6 percent of his passes for 922 yards with three touchdowns and four interceptions in six games.

Should Mayfield not be available, rookie Jalon Daniels would be in line to start on Sunday.

Additionally, Bowles mentioned Yaya Diaby is trending in the right direction to play on Sunday. Safety Antoine Winfield Jr. is the only Tampa Bay player currently ruled out for Week 11.

item.title: Puka Nacua will undergo knee surgery and likely miss the rest of the season
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Sean McVay says Nacua will miss "a couple months."
item.content:encoded:
With the football-following world still processing the fact that Rams receiver Puka Nacua will be able to serve a three-game suspension while on injured reserve (and missing at least four games), Nacua apparently will miss more than the minimum.

Via Nate Atkins of The Athletic, coach Sean McVay said Friday that Nacua will undergo surgery to repair a torn ACL and likely will miss the rest of the season.

Per McVay, Nacua is out "a couple months."

In two months exactly, the divisional round will be looming. The Rams will have to get to the playoffs — and past the divisional round — without him.

Then, the question will be whether he's ready for the round of eight. And so on, for as long as the Rams survive.

Meanwhile, Rams receiver Davante Adams remains on IR with a hamstring injury.

This week, the Rams are on a bye. They host the Packers on Wednesday night, followed by games against the Chiefs, 49ers, Cowboys, Seahawks, Buccaneers, and Seahawks.

item.title: Rookie TE Marlin Klein scores first career TD, Texans lead 26-3
item.dc:creator: Charean Williams
item.description: C.J.
item.content:encoded:
C.J. Stroud threw his third touchdown of the night, giving the Texans a 26-3 lead on the Colts with 4:19 left in the third quarter.

Stroud hit rookie tight end Marlin Klein for a 13-yard score. It was Klein's first career touchdown.

Klein had only one catch this season but has four for 24 yards tonight.

Stroud is 18-of-23 for 179 yards with three touchdowns and an interception.

The Texans led 17-3 at halftime but got a safety when Will Anderson sacked Daniel Jones in the end zone. Anderson leads the NFL with 11.5 sacks, a half sack short of his career high from last season.

The Colts have lost running back Seth McGowan, who was ruled out with a hamstring injury. Tight end Tyler Warren left the game late in the first half and remains on the sideline, but the Colts have not provided an update.

item.title: Shane Steichen on Daniel Jones remaining the starter: "We'll evaluate everything"
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Anthony Richardson could finally get a chance to show what he can do.
item.content:encoded:
As the Colts continue to struggle offensively, they continue to cling to quarterback Daniel Jones.

That may not last for long.

Asked by reporters after the 26-3 loss to the Texans whether Jones will remain the starter, coach Shane Steichen said, "We'll evaluate everything."

The No. 2 quarterback is 2023 top-five pick Anthony Richardson. On Thursday night, he got a garbage-time drive in the fourth quarter. The three-and-out, which started at the Indianapolis 39, consisted of Richardson running for two yards and throwing two incomplete passes.

It was Richardson's second appearance of the season; in Week 8, he got a couple of mop-up drives when the Colts trailed the Jaguars, 42-7.

At some point, Richardson deserves a real chance to play. How much worse can the Colts' offense be?

The Colts were outgained by the Texans, 354 yards to 167. They converted one of 11 third-down tries. Jones completed 12 of 27 passes, for 144 yards, no touchdowns, and an interception.

There's a business reason that points to the Colts eventually getting Jones off the field. His contract has a $10.51 million injury guarantee for 2027. It vests in March. They'll inevitably bench Jones to keep him from getting an injury that would keep the Colts from releasing him before the injury guarantee converts to a full guarantee.

That's what the Giants did to Jones two years ago. He then requested, and received, his release.

The same thing could be happening, sooner rather than later, for Jones in Indianapolis. Which means that he could be available to another team.

That possibility highlights the Colts' decision to not trade him for whatever they could get. And maybe they tried.

Maybe, in the end, his availability in trade is what helped the Vikings keep the Raiders' asking price for Kirk Cousins to a third-round pick.

And maybe, in the end, the Vikings will have a chance to add Jones to the depth chart while showing Carson Wentz the door.

item.title: Jets improved their special teams coverage by having fullback Andrew Beck handle kickoffs
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: Only one kickoff has been returned for a touchdown in the NFL this season, and it was allowed by the Jets when kicker Austin McNamara not only failed to make the tackle, but got in the way of his teammates as they tried to run down Raiders return man Dylan Laube.
item.content:encoded:
Only one kickoff has been returned for a touchdown in the NFL this season, and it was allowed by the Jets when kicker Austin McNamara not only failed to make the tackle, but got in the way of his teammates as they tried to run down Raiders return man Dylan Laube. That got the Jets thinking they needed to improve their kickoff coverage.

The solution was taking kickoff duties away from both McNamara, who is the Jets' punter, and Jason Sanders, who is the Jets' field goal kicker. Instead, it's now fullback Andrew Beck, who has been a good special teams player for years in the NFL, who is handling kickoffs. Beck made a tackle last week on what could have been a much longer kickoff return without him, and he said he loves being able to both kick and make the tackle afterward.

“It was the whole reason that I’m out there, and I think it proves that it’s beneficial to have me doing it,” Beck told Newsday. “Instead of just to get some cool pictures, I’m actually out there doing it for a reason.”

Jets coach Aaron Glenn said when players have a skill set like Beck, with the ability to both kick and tackle, teams need to take advantage of that.

“He’s a unique player that has done a little bit of everything throughout his career,” Glenn said. “We want to utilize that as much as we can.”

Beck kicked in high school but not in college, and he didn't think he'd be kicking again in the NFL. Now that he has the job, however, he hopes it increases his value to the team, and bolsters his career.

“I think I’ve shown that I can be successful in a couple different positions,” he said. “Hopefully the coaches feel comfortable putting me there.”

It's almost unheard of for a player whose primary job isn't punter or kicker to handle kickoffs, although with the dynamic kickoff rule promoting returns, it makes sense for a player who can make tackles to be out there if he's capable of kicking the ball into the landing zone reliably. Saints safety Justin Reid has also kicked off, although he's only done it once this season. If the Jets have success with Beck, it might be something that other teams try — and it might make players who have the unique skill set of being both good kickers and good tacklers more valuable.

item.title: NFLPA names 49ers DL Osa Odighizuwa their Community MVP for Week 11
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: The NFL Players Association announced on Friday that they have named 49ers defensive lineman Osa Odighizuwa as their Community MVP for Week 11.
item.content:encoded:
The NFL Players Association announced on Friday that they have named 49ers defensive lineman Osa Odighizuwa as their Community MVP for Week 11.

Odighizuwa, who was also a Community MVP last season, recently held events in Dallas, San Jose and Portland. Odighizuwa's foundation teamed with Progressive Insurance to provide a new car to a veteran in Dallas and Odighizuwa distributed 500 turkeys in the other two cities to local residents.

“I appreciate everything the NFLPA does for us as players, and I’m honored to be named the Week 11 NFLPA Community MVP,” Odighizuwa said. “Giving back to Portland, Dallas and the Bay Area means a lot to me because each of those communities has played a part in my journey. I hope this recognition encourages my fellow union members to use their platforms to lift others up in the communities they call home.”

The NFLPA will donate $10,000 to Odighizuwa's foundation and he will join the other weekly MVPs in being eligible for the Alan Page Award at the end of the season.

item.title: The Protect College Sports Act proponents are getting desperate
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: As the Protect College Sports Act languishes in the lame-duck session of the U.S.
item.content:encoded:
As the Protect College Sports Act languishes in the lame-duck session of the U.S. House of Representatives, the folks who hope to cure the "chaos" in college sports with an antitrust exemption that will give the NCAA and its members a license to violate the rights of players are getting desperate.

The best evidence of this comes from the fact that New York Yankees president Randy Levine, who serves as the vice-chair of President Trump’s Saving College Sports Roundtable, has called out Stephen A. Smith and me for our public opposition to the PCSA.

We're being challenged by Levine because we've been vocal about calling the PCSA what it is — a bill that addresses the so-called "chaos" in college sports by reducing the rights that the players have won in recent years by successfully attacking a system that was littered with antitrust violations. The powers-that-be want Congress to wave a magic wand that will allow antitrust violations to occur without consequence. (I won't speak for Stephen A. as to why he opposes the PCSA; I respect the fact that he's willing to take a stand that clearly conflicts with the position of his employer.)

Levine made his case against Stephen A. (and Michael J.) in an interview with Charles Gasparino of the New York Post.

"One thing that has really annoyed me is the bogus argument put out by agents and their pundits such as Stephen A. Smith of ESPN and Mike Florio of NBC," Levine said, adding that we "continually misrepresent that student athletes have had and will have no voice, and that is untrue."

The problem isn't they'll have "no voice" later. It's that they have "no voice" now. The process is being run not by the players but by the NCAA and the schools. The players aren't claiming that there's "chaos"; they benefit from the collapse of decades of antitrust violations flowing from the simple fact that the various schools huddled under the umbrella of the NCAA, which issued strict rules limiting what players can receive in exchange for playing college football.

Also, the characterization of me as one of "their pundits" means that Levine believes my opinions aren't the product of my own authentic beliefs but that I'm somehow in the pockets of the agents representing college football players. While that is just plain false, the accusation isn't surprising. We've caught wind of at least one media member who was offered a significant payment for a social-media post supporting the Protect College Sports Act. (I don't know who specifically made the offer, but I know it was made.)

Levine called me in September, on the same day that Senator Ted Cruz (R-Texas) showed up on ESPN's College GameDay to promote the PCSA. Levine began by basically calling me stupid for not realizing that collective bargaining is an impossibility for college sports.

Meanwhile, his November 10, 2026, letter to the entire U.S. House of Representatives explains on page 2 that "there will be nothing to prevent collective bargaining" if the PCSA passes. So if it's stupid for me to think collective bargaining is possible, why would he feel compelled to sell the House on the idea that the PCSA would allow for collective bargaining?

Near the bottom of the article, Levine says this: "I've reached out to both of them (Smith and Florio) to debate me on this issue and heard crickets."

I didn't recall a specific invitation to debate Levine on the issue. I re-read the text message he sent on September 12, after I posted the article regarding our conversation. (It was actually very friendly.) "Always willing to debate and as I said to you in the beginning of the call I just wanted you to have the facts," he wrote. "Was not trying to change your opinion."

I didn't interpret that as an invitation to have a public debate. I thought he meant he's willing to continue to discuss the situation privately. I'm willing to do either, or both.

One last point. Gasparino's article concludes by saying, "Reps for Smith and Florio had no immediate comment."

Here's my immediate comment: I have reps?

I'm easy to find, and I haven't received any request from Gasparino about my position on the PCSA. Which I hope will not exit the House — and which I hope will disappear.

You broke it, you fix it. That should be the message to college sports. Congress has far better things to do, starting with figuring out how to avert an AI-triggered apocalypse.

Which I wish were an exaggeration.

item.title: David Montgomery credits the offensive line after his first big game as a Texan
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: Montgomery totaled 124 yards as the Texans beat the Colts, 26-3.
item.content:encoded:
The Texans traded for running back David Montgomery this offseason, and through the first 10 weeks of the season, he hadn't contributed much of anything. That changed on Thursday night.

Montgomery had 26 carries for 107 yards, plus three catches for 17 yards, as the Texans beat the Colts, 26-3. Montgomery nearly doubled his previous season-high for yardage, and he averaged 4.1 yards per carry after having previously never averaged more than three yards per carry as a Texan.

Afterwards, Montgomery gave the credit to the offensive line, which has been subjected to quite a bit of criticism this season.

“Everybody on our offense, on the O-line, we should believe now because we can do it as long as we stick together and we stick to fundamentals,” Montgomery said, via the Houston Chronicle. “With them guys up front, they catch a lot of heat. They did a hell of a job.”

At 4-6 the Texans still have an uphill battle to make the playoffs. But they traded for Montgomery in the hopes that he could have big games late in the season while they're fighting for a playoff berth, and on Thursday night, Montgomery and the Texans' offensive line did that.

item.title: Christian Parker considered not staying with the Cowboys
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: The Cowboys have removed play-calling duties from defensive coordinator Christian Parker.
item.content:encoded:
The Cowboys have removed play-calling duties from defensive coordinator Christian Parker. Parker initially considered leaving the team. He decided not to.

Parker told reporters on Thursday that he decided to process the "significant" disappointment by remaining in his job, albeit with the most important role taken away.

"That would have been running from it," Parker said as to the possibility of resigning.

As to whether it will be awkward moving forward, Parker said, "I think it's only awkward if you make it, and we don't have to make it that way."

But it will be awkward. The defensive coordinator isn't fully coordinating the defense. And it's not like the situation in Denver, where the head coach assumed the play-calling duties from the coordinator. Parker's biggest responsibilities were given to someone other than the head coach — a consultant who arrived just last month.

The cleanest approach for the Cowboys, given the team's obvious lack of confidence in Parker, would have been to fire him. But that would have come with a buyout of the balance of his contract. And owner/G.M. Jerry Jones doesn't like paying coaches to not work.

Jones likely hopes Parker will eventually realize that the situation isn't sustainable and (as the lingo goes) "self-select." That avoids the buyout and conclusively ends the inherently awkward situation.

item.title: C.J. Stroud: I knew what kind of player I could be, amazing to be in this groove
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: After a rough end to the 2025 season, Texans quarterback C.J.
item.content:encoded:
After a rough end to the 2025 season, Texans quarterback C.J. Stroud came into the 2026 season needing to show he was capable of the kind of consistent production that would land him a big contract extension from the team.

The Texans' overall season hasn't played out as hoped in Houston, but it's not because Stroud has fallen short. He's putting together his best NFL season and it continued with three touchdown passes in Thursday night's win over the Colts.

It was Stroud's third straight game with at least three touchdown passes and it's the first time that Stroud has put together a stretch like that since entering the league.

"I knew what type of player I could be in this league," Stroud said, via DJ Bien-Amie of ESPN.com. "And to just get in that groove and have a rhythm, it's been amazing. Honestly, I would be lying to you if I said it didn't feel good."

Stroud is one off his career high for touchdowns in a season and on pace for a career high in passing yards as well, which makes him a leading reason for the Texans to hope that they can win enough games to get back to the postseason.

item.title: Puka Nacua serving suspension while on IR raises an important question
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: The news that Rams receiver Puka Nacua will serve a three-game suspension while on injured reserve raised plenty of eyebrows, because on the surface it seems very convenient.
item.content:encoded:
The news that Rams receiver Puka Nacua will serve a three-game suspension while on injured reserve raised plenty of eyebrows, because on the surface it seems very convenient.

It seems convenient because it is convenient. More accurately, it's strategic.

The suspension is the result of a negotiation between the league and Nacua. In lieu of taking the process to a full-blown hearing before Judge Sue L. Robinson, whose findings of fact (e.g., "no violation was committed") cannot be appealed by the NFL to the Commissioner, the two sides reached a compromise. They made a deal.

It happens every day in civil and criminal courts throughout the country. Controversies get resolved by negotiation. The mutual uncertainty — one side will win, one side will lose — becomes an outcome that, ideally, both sides don't like but they'll accept.

So the league, which may have been concerned that Nacua wouldn't be suspended at all, agreed to a three-game suspension. Given the timing of the deal, the league necessarily agreed to let Nacua serve the suspension while otherwise unable to play.

The NFL didn't have to do that. It could have dragged its feet. It could have rolled the dice on the decision to be made by Judge Sue L. Robinson. The league ultimately negotiated, and accepted, a situation that allows Nacua to engineer the process in a way that suspends him at a time when he otherwise wouldn't be playing.

The league realizes that many will disagree with the outcome. That's why the initial statement regarding the suspension was followed by an email that said this:

"A player’s injury designation does not delay discipline or prevent a suspension from being served.

"Consistent with prior cases, the suspension begins when it is imposed.

"There is precedent for players serving suspensions while on Reserve/Injured or otherwise unavailable because of injury. This is not a new rule or an exception created for Nacua.

"• Daniel Ekuale, Pittsburgh, 2025 season, was suspended five games for a violation of the performance-enhancing substances policy following a season-ending injury.

"• Sam Williams, Dallas, 2024 season, was suspended three games for violating the personal conduct policy while already out for the season.

"• Mike Woods, Cleveland, 2023, was suspended six games for violating the personal conduct policy while he was out on NFI.

"• David Parry, New Orleans, 2018, was suspended four games for violations of the personal conduct and substances of abuse policies while on injured reserve."

Indeed, Chiefs receiver Rashee Rice had hoped to serve his Personal Conduct Policy suspension for a street-racing incident during the 2024 season, while he was on injured reserve due to a serious knee injury suffered in Week 4. (That didn't happen, because Rice's lawyers were unable to get the prosecutors to finalize the plea deal until after the 2024 season ended.) Similarly, kicker Justin Tucker served his full 10-game suspension in 2025 while not employed by any NFL team.

Here's the philosophical question that the NFL could in theory revisit: Should certain suspensions only be served by a player who is healthy enough to play?

The current system allows players to navigate the process in a way that allows suspensions to be served while the player is injured. And, again, the league chose to resolve the Nacua case at a time when he was injured. The league could have insisted on a suspension that begins once he's healthy, as part of the negotiation. Ultimately, the league exercised the discretion that is inherent to the negotiations that ended the case in a way that allowed to be suspended while injured.

The league could have refused to settle the case in a way that allowed Nacua to serve a suspension while injured. Some will say the league was doing Nacua (and, in turn, the Rams) a favor. The truth may be that the league had real concerns about losing the case before Judge Sue L. Robinson, and that taking a harder line may have resulted in no suspension at all.

Either way, the current system permits it. Moving forward, the league should consider whether — when it comes specifically to the Personal Conduct Policy — it will allow a player to serve a suspension that (while expensive as it relates to the forfeiture of pay) costs the player no playing time.

item.title: Brock Purdy: Practicing at altitude was the right move, for sure
item.dc:creator: Myles Simmons
item.description: When the 49ers play the Vikings this weekend, they'll do so at the altitude of Mexico City at Estadio Banorte.
item.content:encoded:
When the 49ers play the Vikings this weekend, they'll do so at the altitude of Mexico City at Estadio Banorte.

That's why the team is in Colorado Springs this week to practice at the Air Force Academy to get acclimated. The altitude at Colorado Springs is comparable to that of Mexico City, at over 7,000 feet above sea level.

Quarterback Brock Purdy told reporters on Thursday that he appreciates being at altitude this week to prepare.

“It’s a real thing. I think it’s been nice to be here, practice and get some workouts in," Purdy said, via transcript from the team. "Even just obviously doing meetings and just living here for a week. It’s been a real thing that we’ve had to adjust to, and I’m glad that we’re here. I think it’s the right move, for sure. Obviously, Mexico City is going to be in a higher elevation than this, but overall, it’s going to be tough for everybody. We’re not living in it year-round or anything like that, so I don’t know. It’s going to be a part of the game for sure."

Purdy was on the team the last time the 49ers played in Mexico City back in 2022, so he has some understanding of what awaits him. But that was before Jimmy Garoppolo’s injury put Purdy in line to start.

“Obviously, I didn’t play, but just warming up and being there in the game, seeing guys come off the field and seeing them pretty exhausted. It’s a real thing and I think we’re all ready for it,” Purdy said. “For me, I remember those kinds of things, so I’ve just got to be on top of it and prepare for it.”

Kickoff between the Vikings and 49ers is set for 8:20 p.m. ET on Sunday night.

item.title: Ashton Jeanty's bad season running the ball overshadows his receiving production
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: Jeanty is second in the NFL in both catches and receiving yards for a running back this season.
item.content:encoded:
In the time of hot takes, nuanced opinions rarely get much attention, and so in the case of Raiders running back Ashton Jeanty, little has been said about him this season other than that he's a bust. Last year the Raiders took Jeanty with the sixth overall pick in the NFL draft, and this year he's averaging 3.09 yards per carry, worst in the NFL among the 34 running backs with at least 70 carries this season.

First running back drafted to last running back in the yards-per-carry rankings? Bust. Case closed.

Except it's not that simple. There's no excusing the Raiders' awful rushing offense and Jeanty's role in it, but it's also unfair to talk about Jeanty without acknowledging that he's one of the best receivers out of the backfield in the NFL.

Jeanty has 46 catches this season, second only to Cincinnati's Chase Brown among NFL running backs. And Jeanty has 417 receiving yards, second only to San Francisco's Christian McCaffrey. There are a lot of running backs who get praised for what they can contribute in the passing game -- Detroit's Jahmyr Gibbs, Atlanta's Bijan Robinson, Pittsburgh's Jaylen Warren -- and Jeanty has produced more in the passing game than all of them.

Jeanty's 17 receiving first downs are tied with McCaffrey for the most of any running back in the NFL this season. Although Jeanty has only one rushing touchdown this season, he has three receiving touchdowns, tied for the second-most among NFL running backs. (Kansas City's Kenneth Walker has four.)

On Sunday against the Seahawks, when Raiders rookie quarterback Fernando Mendoza struggled in his first NFL start, Jeanty was his leading receiver, with four catches for 46 yards. With the Raiders trying to mount a comeback in the fourth quarter, it was Jeanty turning a short pass into a 38-yard gain that got the Raiders into range for the field goal that made it a one-possession game. The Raiders lost, and Jeanty deserves his share of the blame for their inability to do anything on the ground, but the loss would have been worse if not for Jeanty being available as an outlet receiver for Mendoza.

Jeanty hasn't been the player the Raiders thought they were getting after he was college football's leading rusher at Boise State. But his contributions to the Raiders' offense are real, even if they're not spectacular.

item.title: Thursday Night Football: C.J. Stroud, Texans lead Colts 17-3 at halftime
item.dc:creator: Charean Williams
item.description: Stroud threw two touchdown passes in the first half.
item.content:encoded:
The Texans are doing what they need to do. Now, can they finish?

Four days after blowing a 17-0 lead over the Browns, Houston leads Indianapolis 17-3 at halftime.

The Texans outgained the Colts 202 to 125 in the first half but settled for Ka'imi Fairbairn's 27-yard field goal after stalling at the Indianapolis 9 in the closing seconds.

C.J. Stroud went 13-of-18 for 134 yards with two touchdowns and an interception. He now ranks third in team history in passing yards, surpassing David Carr (13,391).

He has 21 touchdown passes, two short of his career high for a season.

Stroud's touchdowns covered 42 yards to Nico Collins and 24 yards to Kayshon Boutte.

David Montgomery, who missed the previous four games with a groin injury, has 11 carries for 54 yards. Collins has two catches for 48 yards and a touchdown.

The Colts had four plays of over 20 yards, but went 0-for-1 in the red zone, missed two field goals and threw an interception.

The Colts scored their only points on Spencer Shrader's 34-yard field goal. But he missed from 56 and had a 62-yarder blocked by Logan Hall with 2:41 remaining in the half.

Daniel Jones was only 1-for-5 for 22 yards with an interception in the second quarter. He finished the half 7-of-17 for 109 yards and an interception.

Jonathan Taylor has eight carries for 17 yards.

Texans offensive tackle Trent Brown was questionable to return with a back injury. He had been alternating with Braden Smith at right tackle, but Smith played most of the half. Brown, though, did return before the half ended.

Texans defensive tackle Sheldon Rankins is questionable with an ankle injury.

item.title: Aidan Hutchinson: That's the last time I go airborne
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: Lions head coach Dan Campbell said he isn't going to tell players to stop celebrating big plays because of defensive end Aidan Hutchinson's torn ACL, but Hutchinson is going to be making some changes on his own.
item.content:encoded:
Lions head coach Dan Campbell said he isn't going to tell players to stop celebrating big plays because of defensive end Aidan Hutchinson's torn ACL, but Hutchinson is going to be making some changes on his own.

In a post to his Instagram account, Hutchinson made his first public comments since suffering his injury last Sunday. Hutchinson leaped in the air after sacking Patriots quarterback Drake Maye and his knee went out upon landing.

Hutchinson wrote that he has "jumped hundreds of times on a football field and never in a million years did I think this would happen to me" and that it will "never make sense" why things played out the way that they did. He added that he does know he will come back stronger from the injury and "that's the last time I go airborne."

Hutchinson closed the post with a message asking his Lions teammates to "hold down the fort til I’m back." That won't be until 2027, but Hutchinson has shown once already that he can make a full recovery from this kind of injury so there is some light at the end of the tunnel in Detroit.

item.title: As he did with the Giants, Colts QB Daniel Jones is struggling, right after getting paid
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: Jones was awful again in Thursday night's loss to the Texans.
item.content:encoded:
Daniel Jones' career has had some ups, but also plenty of downs, both with the Giants and with the Colts. He has a knack for having his "ups" in contract years, and his "downs" after getting paid.

Jones was awful in Thursday night's loss to the Texans, continuing the worst season of his career — which comes after the Colts signed him to a two-year, $88 million contract in the offseason.

It's not the first time Jones has performed poorly after getting a big deal. In fact, that's all Jones has done throughout his NFL career.

Jones' career started when the Giants made the surprising decision to select him with the sixth overall pick in the 2019 NFL draft. That earned him a four-year, $25.7 million contract, with the Giants having a fifth-year option. Jones didn't live up to expectations on that rookie contract, and was playing some of the worst football of his career when his third season ended early with a neck injury, so the Giants declined his fifth-year option.

But Jones then played very well in his fourth year, leading the Giants to a surprise playoff berth and a win in the wild card round. That led the Giants to sign him to a four-year, $160 million contract in 2023, committing more money to him than his fifth-year option would have cost. Jones responded to that with a fifth season in which he played poorly, suffered another neck injury and then suffered a season-ending torn ACL.

Jones returned in 2024 but was so bad the Giants first benched him, then cut him. Jones spent the rest of that season on the Vikings' practice squad.

In 2025 the Colts signed him to a one-year contract, and he responded by winning a quarterback competition with Anthony Richardson and then playing the best football of his career early in 2025 as the Colts jumped out to an 8-2 start. He started to struggle down the stretch in that season, and then his season was cut short by a torn Achilles tendon, but the Colts were so impressed by his start that they signed him to a two-year, $88 million contract in March.

And now, in the first year of that contract, Jones is worse than ever. His 13 interceptions are the most of any quarterback in the NFL this season and already a career-high, with six more games to play. He's paired that with just seven touchdown passes. He still hasn't had a single game this season with more touchdowns than interceptions. His 65.4 passer rating is a career low. His 30.3 QBR is a career low. His 58.4 percent completion rate is a career low. His 5.6 yards per pass average is a career low. Jones was once an effective runner, but his 2.9 yards per carry average is also a career low. Any way you slice it, Jones is worse than ever.

He's also more expensive than ever. Whether the Colts keep him or cut him, he's going to have a massive salary cap hit in 2027, the kind of cap hit that will make it that much harder for the Colts to rebuild their roster.

If the Colts cut Jones, he may sign another one-year contract with another team. No matter how well he plays, that team would be wise not to give him a lucrative extension.

item.title: Bills to retire Andre Reed's No. 83 in 2027
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: The Bills will be retiring the number of the top wide receiver in franchise history next year.
item.content:encoded:
The Bills will be retiring the number of the top wide receiver in franchise history next year.

Andre Reed piled up more catches, receiving yards and receiving touchdowns than any Bills player while helping the franchise to four straight Super Bowls in the 1990s and the Bills announced that they will be enshrining his No. 83 alongside the numbers of his longtime teammates Jim Kelly, Thurman Thomas and Bruce Smith at some point during the 2027 season. All four players are also in the Pro Football Hall of Fame.

"He's one of the main reasons I'm up on that wall," Kelly said, via the team's website. "He's one of the main reasons I'm in the Pro Football Hall of Fame; it takes both of us. When your quarterback goes in, usually you're probably going to have a receiver or two go in. . . . To have Andre for my whole career was just totally awesome. I thought it should have been done a few years ago, but I'm glad that it's getting done, and I'm glad I'm able to be here and celebrate his going on the wall to join me, Bruce and Thurman."

Reed had 941 catches for 13,095 yards and 86 touchdowns over 15 seasons in Buffalo. He was added to the franchise's Wall of Fame in 2006 and voted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2014.

item.content:encoded:

Collins caught three passes for 58 yards.

Texans running back David Montgomery, who missed four games with a groin injury, had 26 carries for 107 yards in his return. The Texans played without running back Woody Marks, who has a concussion.

Will Anderson had a sack of Daniel Jones in the end zone for a safety, increasing his league-leading sack total to 11.5. Jadeveon Clowney also had a sack, and Kamari Lassiter had a pick of Daniel Jones.

Jones was 12-of-27 for 144 yards and a pick, and Jonathan Taylor rushed for only 21 yards on 11 carries. Anthony Gould made two catches for 48 yards.

The Colts scored their only points on Spencer Shrader’s 34-yard field goal. But he missed from 56 and had a 62-yarder blocked by Logan Hall with 2:41 remaining in the first half.

item.title: Jack Ham will return to Penn State radio booth following medical emergency
item.dc:creator: Charean Williams
item.description: Pro Football Hall of Fame linebacker Jack Ham announced he will return to the Penn State radio booth on Saturday, two weeks after a medical emergency.
item.content:encoded:
Pro Football Hall of Fame linebacker Jack Ham announced he will return to the Penn State radio booth on Saturday, two weeks after a medical emergency.

Ham, a color analyst for the Penn State Sports Network since 2000, was transported to the University of Washington Medical Center during pregame of the Nittany Lions' Nov. 7 game. He missed Penn State's game against Minnesota last week.

I've spent a lot of Saturdays in Beaver Stadium, first on the field and then up in the booth," Ham, 77, said in his statement. "I'll be back alongside Steve [Jones] this weekend, and there's nowhere else I'd rather be."

Jones treated Ham at the scene, saving his life, according to Penn State coach Matt Campbell. Ham remained in the hospital several days before returning to Pennsylvania on Saturday.

"I'm feeling good, and I owe a great deal to the people who took care of me and stood by me through all of it," Ham said.

Ham was a six-time All-Pro with the Steelers, with whom he won four Super Bowl championships. He also made eight Pro Bowl appearances. He earned All-America honors at Penn State in 1970.

He entered the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 1988 and the College Football Hall of Fame two years later.

item.title: Vikings explored all options before deciding to stay in Minnesota this week
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: As Sunday's Mexico City game between the Vikings and 49ers approaches, one of the big issues is the decision of the 49ers to spend the week at altitude in Colorado Springs while the Vikings opted to stay in Minnesota.
item.content:encoded:
As Sunday's Mexico City game between the Vikings and 49ers approaches, one of the big issues is the decision of the 49ers to spend the week at altitude in Colorado Springs while the Vikings opted to stay in Minnesota.

On that point, multiple 49ers players have claimed that the Vikings tried to secure the Air Force Academy facility at Colorado Springs, but the 49ers had beaten them to the punch.

The Vikings, we're told, explored all options — including going to Air Force Acadamey facility and going to Mexico City early. They ultimately decided to implement a plan premised on staying in Minnesota as long as possible.

Obviously, the Vikings could have figured out something that would have allowed them to spend the week somewhere that would have allowed for full acclimation. There are other practice facilities in Colorado. And, again, early arrival in Mexico was always a possibility.

The issue has likely become a focal point of the days preceding the game because of the dramatically different approaches used by the 49ers and Rams before their Week 1 game in Australia. San Francisco went early; the Rams arrived late. And the 49ers stunned the Rams, 27-7.

In that case, it was about time and distance traveled. Here, it's the same time zone, and the flight is roughly four hours — not much farther for the Vikings than a trip to Seattle, San Francisco, or L.A.

Teams that play in Denver don't spend the week in Colorado. And while the altitude results in more sideline shots of players with oxygen masks during games, no one ever says, "Well, that team lost to the Broncos because they weren't acclimated to the altitude."

The Vikings-49ers game won't turn on that. If the 49ers win, it will be because they were the better team during those 60 minutes of clock time. And, if the Vikings win, it won't be because they someone cracked the code on playing at altitude.

item.title: Puka Nacua's suspension arises from diversion program
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: The NFL's statement announcing the three-game suspension for Rams receiver Puka Nacua didn't specify the reason for it.
item.content:encoded:
The NFL's statement announcing the three-game suspension for Rams receiver Puka Nacua didn't specify the reason for it. Further information provided by the league makes the basis for the ban clear.

It comes from Nacua's entry into a "diversion program," related to the incident that triggered a civil lawsuit alleging (among other things) that he bit a woman on New Year's Eve.

In September, we explained that Nacua had begun the steps required to complete a diversion program, which happened without Nacua entering into a formal agreement to do so. It's one of the unique facets of California law; namely, California gives some defendants the ability to embark on the steps to comply with a diversion program without the kind of express deal that would have automatically triggered review under the Personal Conduct Policy.

The approach ultimately didn't avoid the NFL scrutiny.

The suspension of Nacua for three games, with the acknowledgment from the league that failure "to satisfy the conditions of his diversion program" will result in "additional and more substantial discipline," means that the mere commencement of the process of compliance, even without an express agreement with prosecutors, was enough to get the process rolling.

It also led to a negotiated conclusion that entails Nacua being suspended for games he otherwise would have missed, due to his status on injured reserve. While it all looks convenient at best and fishy at worst, it represents the outcome of a bargain aimed at resolving the situation without full-blown activation of a process that would have entailed a formal hearing before Judge Sue L. Robinson, the person jointly appointed by the NFL and the NFL Players Association to hear the evidence and to issue a preliminary decision.

item.title: C.J. Stroud's second TD gives Texans 14-3 lead
item.dc:creator: Charean Williams
item.description: The Texans took advantage of Kamari Lassiter's interception of Daniel Jones, driving 85 yards in 12 plays for their second touchdown.
item.content:encoded:
The Texans took advantage of Kamari Lassiter's interception of Daniel Jones, driving 85 yards in 12 plays for their second touchdown. They lead the Colts 14-3 with 7:38 remaining in the second quarter.

C.J. Stroud hit Kayshon Boutte, who was well covered by Kenneth Harris, for a 24-yard touchdown on third-and-2.

It was Stroud's second touchdown pass of the night and his 21st of the season.

The Texans have 155 yards, with Stroud going 11-of-13 for 118 yards with two touchdowns and an interception.

He has completed a pass to seven different receivers, led by Nico Collins' 48 yards on two catches. Collins scored the team's first touchdown on a 42-yard reception.

item.title: C.J. Stroud connects with Nico Collins to give Texans 7-3 lead
item.dc:creator: Charean Williams
item.description: The Texans were outplayed for most of the first quarter, but they have a 7-3 lead.
item.content:encoded:
The Texans were outplayed for most of the first quarter, but they have a 7-3 lead.

Spencer Shrader kicked a 34-yard field but missed from 56, giving the Colts an early 3-0 lead. They had drives of nine plays, 44 yards and eight plays, 35 yards.

The Colts defense, missing cornerbacks Charvarius Ward and Sauce Gardner, intercepted C.J. Stroud on the Texans' first drive. It was a fluke pick, first hitting AJ Haulcy in the helmet, then off the hands of Cam Bynum before landing back in Haulcy's hands.

The Texans, though, answered on their second drive.

Stroud avoided the blitz of cornerback Kapena Gushiken, who grabbed a piece of Stroud's jersey, by stepping up in the pocket before heaving a dime into the end zone to Nico Collins. Collins was covered by Justin Walley, but it was no match.

The 42-yard touchdown pass gave the Texans their first lead.

It was Stroud's 20th touchdown. His career high is 23.
